summary: The Cure Hepatitis C Act of 2026 establishes a national program led by the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) to eliminate the hepatitis C virus in the United States. It creates a five-year subscription model for purchasing hepatitis C treatments, provides medications without cost-sharing for high-risk or vulnerable populations (including individuals in Medicaid, CHIP, correctional facilities, the Indian Health Service, and the uninsured), and sets up grants, testing resources, public awareness campaigns, and cost-sharing removals for Medicare beneficiaries.

affected_groups.effect: Individuals enrolled in participating state Medicaid or CHIP programs who have hepatitis C are entitled to receive treatments without cost-sharing.

Individuals confined in federal, participating state, or local correctional facilities can receive hepatitis C treatments without cost-sharing, and receive remaining treatment and referral upon release.
Individuals without minimum essential coverage who are diagnosed with hepatitis C can receive treatments without cost-sharing through designated healthcare providers and registered pharmacies.
Individuals receiving healthcare through the Indian Health Service or tribal programs are eligible for the treatment program, and tribal health facilities are eligible for elimination grants.
affected_groups.group: Indian Health Service and Tribal Populations

affected_groups.effect: Beneficiaries enrolled in Medicare Part D will have no deductibles or cost-sharing for direct acting antivirals treating hepatitis C from plan years 2028 through 2032.
Manufacturers of hepatitis C treatments participate in competitive bidding for five-year subscription purchase contracts with HHS.

key_provisions: Establishes a Hepatitis C Elimination Program requiring HHS to issue a national strategy, advisory committee, interagency working group, and a public progress dashboard.
Directs HHS to enter into five-year subscription contracts with drug manufacturers to purchase hepatitis C treatments in bulk for covered populations.

Provides hepatitis C treatments without cost-sharing for eligible individuals in participating state Medicaid and CHIP programs, participating state/local correctional systems, federal prisons, Indian health programs, and uninsured individuals.
Eliminates cost-sharing and deductibles for direct-acting antivirals treating hepatitis C under Medicare Part D for plan years 2028 through 2032.

Authorizes grants and contracts to states, public health departments, community health centers, opioid treatment programs, correctional facilities, and Ryan White clinics to support testing, treatment, and wraparound services.

Provides mandatory federal appropriations of $5,500,000,000 for fiscal year 2027 to remain available through fiscal year 2033 for the subscription program, and $4,283,000,000 for fiscal year 2027 for other elimination activities.
missing_information: Specific criteria or formulas the Secretary will use to determine the best value bids from drug manufacturers.
Exact details on how the state allocation formula for public health grants will weigh specific disease burdens.
summary_detail.plain_summary: The Cure Hepatitis C Act of 2026 establishes a national program led by the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) to eliminate the hepatitis C virus in the United States. It creates a five-year subscription model for purchasing hepatitis C treatments, provides medications without cost-sharing for high-risk or vulnerable populations (including individuals in Medicaid, CHIP, correctional facilities, the Indian Health Service, and the uninsured), and sets up grants, testing resources, public awareness campaigns, and cost-sharing removals for Medicare beneficiaries.
summary_detail.significance: The bill represents a sweeping federal initiative to eliminate hepatitis C by investing billions of dollars in bulk drug purchasing, widespread testing, public awareness campaigns, and the complete removal of out-of-pocket costs for vulnerable and high-risk populations across public health programs, corrections, and Medicare.
